newsitem.title: BELARUS: Lukashenko urges speedier integration with Russia.
newsitem.headline: Lukashenko urges speedier integration with Russia.

text.p: Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko, fresh from talks with Russian President Boris Yeltsin on closer union, urged parliaments of both states to help speed up integration.

"I propose that you, energetically and quickly, concentrate on approving a citizenship (law) of the community," he told a meeting of 25 deputies from each country in a speech which stressed Belarus' desire to maintain its territorial integrity.

"Every citizen of Russia and Belarus is a citizen of the community and of his own country...This will secure freedom of movement, equal citizens' rights in the two states and equal participation in elections," he said.
The hardline leader repeated criticism of Russia for slow progress in integration since he and Yeltsin signed a pact on forming an economic "community" in April.
"Today I propose to Russia: let us create a union following the formula of two states, two voices. But Russia is not ready for this," he said.
His speech was interrupted by applause from Russian deputies.

Among them was the chairman of the State Duma lower house, communist Gennady Seleznyov, and reformist Moscow mayor Yuri Luzhkov. member of the Federation Council upper house who is widely seen as a potential candidate in the next presidential election due in the year 2000.
"Russia is not ready for union today without incorporating the north-western region. But the Belarussian people will not agree to that," Lukashenko said.
Lukashenko met Yeltsin last Friday and the two signed a declaration that called for integration of their customs, fiscal, transport and energy systems and synchronisation of economic reforms.
Lukashenko's go-slow approach to reform has led to international lending bodies suspending credits to Belarus.
His policy of forming some kind of union with Russia helped to put him in power though it is opposed by a noisy sector who accuse him of ignoring democratic principles to shore up his leadership.
The latest protest against his policies on Monday ended in angry scuffles with police, at least two injuries and about 100 arrests, opposition leaders said.
In typically critical comments on Western plans to expand the NATO alliance eastwards, Lukashenko said an alternative alliance could be set up between China, Russia and Belarus.

"We have discussed the possibility with the Chinese leadership of a Beijing-Moscow-Minsk axis. This would be a strategic axis, an air corridor, our answer to NATO expansion. We can find many answers," he said.
Russia and China, who seek to improve political and economic ties, have consistently rejected any idea of forming a military bloc.

Lukashenko, who once called NATO a monster, accused the West of setting up electronic intelligence monitoring equipment on the Polish and Lithuanian borders of his former Soviet republic of 10 million.
